headline: A Recursive Time Helix That Winds from Centuries to Seconds
lede: When a former Pixar lighting technologist sketches an idea on X and a browser shader artist builds it in real-time three dimensions, the result belongs to a surprisingly deep tradition of computational cartography. The prototype — a recursive time helix whose nested coils scale from centuries down to individual seconds — navigates to 45 BCE at timestamp precision, and runs entirely inside a browser tab.
body:
The governing idea is elegant: a **helix** unifies the two ways people intuitively experience time. A circle captures recurrence — Tuesday follows Monday in an endless loop — but erases forward motion. A straight line captures progress but loses the sense that this October resembles last October. The helix does both: it advances along a linear axis while revolving through cycles, so the same angular position at every altitude corresponds to the same season, the same hour, the same minute. Nest enough helixes — centuries riding on decades, decades on years, years on days — and you have a coordinate system for all of recorded history that a user navigates by spinning and zooming rather than scrolling a flat bar.

The conceptual lineage is longer than the prototype's age suggests. In 1997, geographers Robert Edsall and Donna Peuquet proposed the *Time Coil* within a GIS system — a helical path whose linear axis encoded irreversible progression while its revolutions encoded periodic return. Four years later, Marc Weber, Marc Alexa, and Wolfgang Müller formalized the *spiral time plot* in a landmark IEEE InfoVis paper, demonstrating that spirals reveal periodicities invisible in linear charts. The commercial high-water mark arrived with **Helixaeon** (private), whose 2016 patent describes a parent-child architecture in which each child helix uses the parent's path as its own central axis — precisely the *recursive coil* structure codetaur implements. What no prior system managed was to run in real time inside a browser, interactively, with the geometry itself tunable through a live parameter panel.

The technical moment making this feasible is the browser's recent acquisition of **WebGPU** — the successor to *WebGL*, finally exposing modern GPU APIs (Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12) to JavaScript. Safari 26, released in September 2025, completed WebGPU's cross-browser rollout; Three.js r171, the same month, made WebGPU zero-configuration by default. The implications for projects like this are concrete: *compute shaders* allow the helix positions for millions of nested points to be calculated on the GPU in parallel, while *TSL* (Three Shading Language) compiles the same shader code to both WebGPU and the older WebGL backend automatically. What once required a research lab's rendering pipeline now ships in a script tag.

The collaboration captures something specific about the current creative-coding moment. Tim Babb (@tr_babb) — a former lighting technology lead at **Pixar Animation Studios** (private) and founder of **Lynxtool** (private), with his own WebGPU framework on GitHub — sketched the idea publicly. Within what appears to be a short interval, codetaur (whose CRT shader work has been retweeted by Three.js creator Ricardo Cabello) translated the sketch into interactive geometry. The visible interface — sliders for coil density, spacing, tilt, *sec/pixel* (seconds mapped to each screen pixel, the zoom-depth dial), and transition speed — suggests the parametric ambition is genuine rather than cosmetic. The timestamp "-45 BCE 11/17 10:04:47" in the prototype screenshot places the view in the era of Julius Caesar at second-level resolution.

The labels, codetaur notes, still need work. That is almost always where projects like this either mature into something others can use or stall at the boundary between impressive prototype and legible tool. The open question is whether the navigation metaphor — orbiting a coil to find a century, then descending into its child coil for the decade, then the year — can be made intuitive without collapsing into the flat timelines it was designed to replace.

concepts.definition: A three-dimensional helical curve used as a time visualization structure. Its linear axis encodes irreversible forward flow while its revolutions encode repeating cycles (days, seasons, years), unifying the two intuitive modes of temporal experience in one geometric object.

A visualization architecture in which each helix serves as the central axis for a smaller child helix at the next finer temporal scale — centuries contain decade-helixes, which contain year-helixes, and so on. Zooming in reveals the next level of detail without switching to a different view.

The browser graphics API that succeeded WebGL, exposing modern GPU interfaces (Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12) to JavaScript. It enables compute shaders, higher draw-call throughput, and multi-threaded rendering. Became cross-browser viable in late 2025 when Safari added native support.

The previous browser graphics API, based on OpenGL ES, that allowed JavaScript to render 3D graphics using the GPU. Widely supported but limited to an older GPU programming model; being superseded by WebGPU in performance-sensitive applications.

A GPU program that runs general-purpose parallel computation — not just rendering — across thousands of cores simultaneously. In a helix visualization, compute shaders can calculate the 3D positions of millions of nested coil points in a single GPU dispatch, a task that would take far too long on a CPU.

A node-based shader abstraction within Three.js that allows developers to write GPU shader code once and have it compile automatically to WGSL (WebGPU's shader language) or GLSL (WebGL's). Removes the need to maintain two separate codebases for different GPU backends.

A zoom parameter in the prototype UI — seconds per screen pixel — that controls how much time each pixel of the helix represents. Reducing it zooms in to show finer time resolution; increasing it zooms out to encompass longer spans.

A visualization technique, formalized in a 2001 IEEE InfoVis paper by Weber, Alexa, and Müller, that maps a time series along an Archimedean spiral rather than a horizontal axis. Periodic patterns appear as alignment across adjacent loops, revealing regularities that a linear chart would obscure.

A helical time representation proposed by geographers Edsall and Peuquet in 1997 for use in GIS software. Its linear axis encoded the irreversible forward flow of time; its revolutions encoded cyclic return. One of the earliest academic precedents for the helix-as-time-metaphor.

repos.summary: Tim Babb's framework for writing graphics and compute code in WebGPU, written in C++. It reflects his low-level GPU work from his Pixar career and establishes that his time helix sketch came from someone who has implemented WebGPU primitives from scratch, not a casual observer of the technology.

The leading open-source JavaScript 3D library, maintained by Ricardo Cabello and hundreds of contributors since 2010. Abstracts over WebGL and WebGPU so developers write 3D scenes and shaders without touching GPU APIs directly. Used across the creative-coding and data-visualization community for interactive experiences that run entirely in the browser.
